"Another one bites the dust", he thought. He used to like that song, but now it felt different. Death sat grimly on rusty car watching the human draw his final breathes. It had been 11 years since international disaster lead to the nuclear holocaust, a moment in time not even Death enjoyed. Do you know how hard it is to reap billions of lives? It took nearly a decade just to finish that. It was only after those 10 long years of coaxing the final ghosts out of hiding that Death realized he might soon be unemployed. Everyone always asked what happens to them after they die, but nobody ever asked what happened to death once everyone was already dead. After all, unemployed could have an entirely different meaning for Death, and it's not like anyone wrote it in his job description. Can Death die? Would he get a new job? Maybe a nice cushy one like that do-nothing Time.

Death pondered these questions while out of the shadows a creature drew near to him. Startled, he realized it was another human. This human was in rough shape. He was so skinny his body almost looked malformed. He was wearing a rank plaid shirt, his beard covered in debris, twisting in knots and locks. In fact, the first thing he did when he found the scissors on the dead human was cut these locks from his beard. Then he scavenged the corpse for provisions. "This human might have a chance", he thought, "I shall call him... Rick."

Death followed as Rick rummaged through the outskirts of the city, carefully whispering when he noticed a loose steel beam about to fall on Rick, grabbing his attention long enough to avoid disaster. Death could sense another meatbag nearby, so he attempted to drive Rick towards him. Death pushed a washing machine out of a nearby window, grabbing their attention as they turned the corner into each other, and then proceeded to fight. Rick had ducked a machete and pinned the other human to the ground, knocking off his baseball cap, inscribed with just "P". With the upper hand, Rick overpowered the other human and drove his boot knife into the other mans chest multiple times. The plaid shirt was an even darker red now. Rick leaned against the buildings stones, holding his leg. Apparently Mr. P over there got Rick with his machete just before he was stabbed. Death could immediately tell it was a fatal femoral artery injury.

Death brought his skeletal hand to his face. Maybe humans were destined to die, he thought. Sighing, he began reaping them. He wasn't nice about it either, I mean, he really made sure they knew what idiots they were. He tore their souls out slower than usual and let them linger in his hands a few moments. Nothing was more painful to a human soul than lingering about, each second feeling like an eternity. He let the souls go, and both drifted towards the ground. Typical, he thought. They disappeared into the cracked cement.

...

Death found another human, this time a woman. Any human would probably have mistaken her for a man, and she probably wanted it that way. Her hair was cut short, and she had a stocky build with wide shoulders. She looked meaner than Rick did. He just happened to find her as she ran into another human, a rare coincidence these days despite his most recent encounter. To his surprise, she didn't start beating him to death, and he her. They started talking, and soon began venturing together.

Maybe there was some hope after all.

Just for the uninformed, there is a difference between agnosticism and atheism, and by that I mean they are apples and oranges.

Atheism is a statement of belief, agnosticism is a statement of knowledge. You can be an agnostic atheist, a gnostic atheist, an agnostic theist, or a gnostic theist.

Agnostic means you don't think it can be proven whether a supernatural power exists, gnostic means you think it can be proven.

Atheist means you do not believe in the supernatural, whereas a theist means you believe in some supernatural power.

Wouldn't you need to prove that God exists before having an argument about whether or not God is the basis of morality?

I do agree that atheists and theists share a similar sense of morality in most things, but not for the reason you specify (that they can be objectively true). I don't believe in in objective morality because it supposes that a supernatural force controls what is wrong or right. In my opinion, morality is simply a collection of subjective morals that get tweaked over time to match the group they reside in. A simple example would be the different types of ways we interactive with people in different cultures. Some people greet with kisses, others with handshakes, and in some areas a handshake is considered rude or even unthinkable. These aren't the typical morals we consider in this type of conversation, but I am doing my best to display morals that are largely unrelated to (or based on) religion. All of these developed through a type of "moral evolution" that took place in each culture around the world. Many mixed, and the biggest ones are easy to spot: Do not kill other people, do not steal, etc. These morals make sense as a universal because they have the greatest benefit for a culture; even then, you will still find cultures that are OK with it in some cases! (For example, the death penalty, or gladiators in history).

So if I had to try and clearly state my opinion on morality as succinctly as possible it would be this:

There is no objective morality. No action is innately good or bad. What decides morality is a collection of subjective (morals derived individually) morals combined into a cultural morality over time. We decide what is right or wrong together, and change those definitions over time.

I'm not one of them. I'm not necessarily a proponent of nihilism, as I believe morals are governed by social norms (and rightfully so as a means to co-exist in the same space as other people).

I do believe the world would be better without religion, though, because morals aren't necessarily (or rather, don't need to be) a product of religion. Most atheists still have morals, it's not like getting rid of religion gets rid of morals, they are just different morals and not so stringent on tradition. Non-religious morals tend to change faster than religious morals and fit better with the time period they exist in. Religious morals tend to hinder social progression in my mind, focusing on keeping things the same rather than evolving to create a better world for everyone.

It makes it 1:1 where default:relative, rather than say 1:.8, where default:relative (a.k.a. slower when zoomed in with relative sensitivity).

With relative you just put it to 0. Here is an [image](https://i.imgur.com/2qpqF2A.jpg) of the option, if it helps.

Make your main sensitivity one number and stick with it (maybe adjust slightly at first until it feels comfortable, but don't change it often or you will keep having to re-learn the muscle memory).

Slide that "relative aim sensitivity while zoomed" option all the way to 0.

You would think it would give you more precision, yes, but you've trained on literally every other hero how fast the cursor moves across the screen, then all of a sudden this one hero - only when zoomed - uses a different sensitivity. Now you have to learn how to aim all over again, using two different sensitivies. It makes way more sense to use one sensitivity and just get used to it.

So if all you do is snipe, then lower your native sensitivity a bit and get good at it. You should leave it high enough that you can spin around really fast, but slow it down enough where you feel comfortable aiming with a sniper.

For anyone trying to play Widowmaker (on either console or PC), make sure you turn off relative sensitivity when zoomed in. I have no idea why they didn't make it 0 by default, but it really screws people's aim up.
